content.title: Applying Mean and Weighted Mean
content.overview: This lesson covers how to calculate the overall average when combining multiple groups of different sizes. Unlike a simple average, a weighted mean accounts for the specific contribution of each group based on its count.
learning_objectives: Calculate the total sum of a group using its mean and count.
Determine the weighted mean of combined groups with different sizes.
Identify and avoid the 'simple average' trap in multi-group problems.
Verify that a weighted mean falls logically between the component means.

sections.title: The Concept of Total Contribution
sections.content: The mean (average) of a set is the sum of all values divided by the number of items. To find the weighted mean of multiple groups, you must first find the 'total contribution' of each group. This is done by rearranging the average formula: Total Sum = Mean × Count. For example, if 5 students average 80 on a test, their total contribution to the class sum is 400 points.

sections.title: The Weighted Mean Procedure
sections.content:
When merging groups of different sizes, follow these three steps: 1. Multiply each group's mean by its count to find the group's total sum. 2. Add all the group sums together to find the combined total. 3. Divide this combined total by the sum of all counts (the total number of items). This ensures that larger groups have a proportionally larger impact on the final result.

![A flowchart showing the steps: Mean times Count, Sum the Totals, Divide by Total Count.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/c09c153b-d9d9-4ced-bf2c-b31015f2a513-1786506268427-755.webp)

sections.title: The Simple Average Trap
sections.content: A common mistake is taking the 'average of the averages.' If Group A has 10 people and Group B has 90 people, the overall mean will be much closer to Group B's mean. Simply adding the two means and dividing by two ignores the fact that Group B has nine times as many data points. Only use a simple average if all groups have the exact same number of items.

worked_examples.question: A local gym has two yoga classes. The morning class has 20 participants with an average age of 30. The evening class has 30 participants with an average age of 40. What is the average age of all yoga participants at the gym?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find the total contribution of the morning class. 20 participants × 30 years = 600 total years. Step 2: Find the total contribution of the evening class. 30 participants × 40 years = 1,200 total years. Step 3: Find the combined total sum and combined count. Total years = 600 + 1,200 = 1,800. Total participants = 20 + 30 = 50. Step 4: Divide the combined total by the combined count. 1,800 ÷ 50 = 36. The weighted mean age is 36.

common_mistakes: Averaging the means directly (e.g., (30+40)/2 = 35) without accounting for group size.
Dividing the total sum by the number of groups instead of the total number of items.
Forgetting to include individual values if a single new item is added to an existing group mean.
exam_tips: Sanity Check: The weighted mean must always be between the lowest and highest individual group means.
Proximity Rule: The final weighted mean will always be closer to the mean of the group with the larger count.
Look for keywords like 'combined average' or 'overall mean' to trigger the weighted mean strategy.
content.recap: To find a weighted mean, multiply each mean by its count to get total sums, add those sums together, and divide by the total number of items. This prevents larger groups from being underrepresented in the final average.

knowledge_claims.content: The total sum of a group's values is calculated by multiplying the group's mean by the number of items (count) in that group.
To find a weighted mean, first calculate the total sum for each individual group by multiplying mean times count.
After finding individual group sums, add them together to determine the combined total sum of all items.
The final step in calculating a weighted mean is dividing the combined total sum by the sum of all group counts.
Calculating a simple average of group means is incorrect when the groups have different numbers of items.
A valid weighted mean must always fall between the smallest and largest individual group means.
In a weighted mean calculation, the group with the largest count exerts the most influence on the final average.
Weighted mean strategies should be used whenever separate groups with known averages and sizes are merged into one.
A weighted mean equals a simple average only when all groups being combined have the exact same count.
If a single value is added to a group, the new mean is (Original Total Sum + New Value) divided by (Original Count + 1).
If the weighted mean is closer to Group A's mean than Group B's mean, Group A must have a higher count than Group B.
Total contribution refers to the sum of all individual values within a specific group, derived from the mean and count.
